breakfast.name: Plăcinte (Filled Pastries)
ingredients: Filling: brânză (cheese), potatoes, cabbage, or apples
instructions: Make thin elastic dough
Stretch and fill
Fold into squares
Pan-fry in oil until golden
breakfast.description: Thin stretched pastries with cheese or cabbage — Moldova's beloved comfort.

breakfast.name: Mămăligă (Cornmeal Porridge)
instructions: Boil water with salt
Stir in cornmeal, cook until thick
Turn out of pot
Slice with string or knife
Serve with butter, sour cream, and cheese
breakfast.description: Golden cornmeal porridge — Moldova's answer to polenta.

breakfast.name: Mamaliga cu Brânza (Polenta with Cheese)
ingredients: Brânza (traditional Moldovan white sheep cheese — salty)
instructions: Boil water with salt
Add maize flour gradually, stirring to avoid lumps
Stir vigorously and continuously — the mamaliga cooks in 15 minutes
It should be very thick — thick enough to turn out and slice
Turn onto a wooden board — traditional Moldovan mamaliga is cut with a thread, not a knife
Serve with sliced brânza (the salty sheep cheese)
Add smetana (Moldovan sour cream) alongside
Drizzle with melted butter
Mamaliga cu brânza is Moldova's most beloved dish
The combination of hot, dense polenta with salty sharp cheese and cool sour cream is the Moldovan trifecta
Moldova's relationship with mamaliga mirrors Romania's — the shared Eastern European corn heritage
breakfast.description: Moldova's most beloved dish — dense cornmeal polenta cut with a thread (not a knife, the traditional Moldovan way), served with salty sheep brânza and cool sour cream. The mamaliga-cheese-sour cream trifecta is Moldova's comfort food in its purest form. Mamaliga's tradition is shared with Romania (Moldova was part of Romania until 1812 Russian annexation).

breakfast.name: Zeamă de Pui (Chicken Noodle Soup)
instructions: Simmer chicken in cold water from the start — this extracts maximum gelatin and flavor
Add whole vegetables: carrot, onion cut in half, celery, parsley root
Simmer 40 minutes — the broth should be golden and clear
Strain — keep the broth, discard cooked vegetables
Add fresh vegetables cut into small pieces for texture
Add homemade egg noodles (tăiței) — they cook in the broth
Season with salt, pepper, generous fresh dill and parsley
Optional: lovage (leuștean) — Moldova's distinctive herbal addition, earthy and strong
The zeamă is Moldova's Sunday soup — eaten at every family gathering
The lovage herb distinguishes Moldovan zeamă from Romanian ciorba
breakfast.description: Moldova's Sunday soup — slow-simmered chicken broth with homemade egg noodles, dill, parsley, and optionally lovage (leuștean — the herb that distinguishes Moldovan soup from Romanian ciorbă). The golden, clear broth achieved by starting from cold water is the technique. Moldova's version of the universal 'grandmother's chicken soup' with its own herbal identity.

lunch.name: Sarmale (Cabbage Rolls)
instructions: Mix filling
Roll in cabbage leaves
Line pot with sauerkraut
Pack rolls, add tomato paste, water
Simmer 2 hours
Serve with mămăligă and sour cream
lunch.description: Moldovan stuffed cabbage rolls — slow-simmered in sauerkraut.

lunch.name: Zeamă (Chicken Noodle Soup)
instructions: Simmer chicken 30 min
Add vegetables
Add noodles, cook 10 min
Finish with lemon juice and lovage
lunch.description: Clear, tangy chicken noodle soup with lovage — the Moldovan cure-all.

lunch.name: Sarmale (Stuffed Cabbage Rolls)
ingredients: White or sour cabbage (sauerkraut leaves are better — the sourness is essential)
Rice (small amount — not the primary ingredient)
instructions: Separate cabbage leaves — blanch fresh or use sour cabbage leaves as-is
Filling: mix minced meat with onion, garlic, small amount of rice, dill
Season well — the filling should be well-spiced
Place filling on each leaf, roll tightly — tuck ends in
Layer in a pot: some tomato sauce on the bottom, then sarmale
Pack tightly — they hold their shape when packed against each other
Cover with tomato sauce, add bay leaf, thyme
Braise 1.5-2 hours on low heat — low and slow is essential
Sarmale improve overnight — they're better the next day
Serve with smetana and mamaliga or bread
Sarmale is Moldova's and Romania's most important celebration dish
lunch.description: Moldova's celebration stuffed cabbage — minced pork mixed with rice and dill, rolled in sour cabbage leaves, packed tightly and braised for hours in tomato sauce. Sarmale improve overnight (made the day before celebrations). The sour cabbage leaf is the Moldovan/Romanian preference over fresh cabbage — it adds tang that no amount of vinegar in fresh cabbage replicates.

lunch.name: Piftie (Aspic of Pig's Feet)
ingredients: Optional: carrot for color in the aspic
instructions: Simmer pig's feet, ears, and knuckle in water with bay leaf and peppercorns — 3 hours minimum
The long cooking extracts enormous amounts of gelatin from bones and skin
The broth becomes very thick with gelatin — this is the aspic base
Remove all bones and skin from the cooked pork — shred the meat
Add very generous garlic to the cooking liquid — the garlic flavor permeates the piftie
Strain the broth
Place shredded meat in molds or bowls
Pour strained broth over — it should be deeply flavorful and gelatinous
Refrigerate overnight — the gelatin sets completely
Slice and serve cold — the aspic is jiggly, firm, and garlic-intense
Piftie is Moldova's winter celebration food — made for Christmas and New Year
The pig is slaughtered in December — piftie uses the parts that don't keep otherwise
lunch.description: Moldova's Christmas aspic — pig's feet and ears boiled for hours until the gelatin-rich broth sets around shredded pork in a mold. Generously garlicked and served cold in slices. Made from the December pig slaughter using the gelatin-rich parts. Piftie improves over days in the cold cellar. The jiggly, garlic-intense cold aspic is Moldova's winter celebration dish.

dinner.name: Tochitura (Pork Stew)
instructions: Brown pork cubes
Add garlic, wine, tomato sauce
Simmer 30 min
Serve on mămăligă with fried egg and cheese
dinner.description: Rich pork stew on mămăligă with egg and cheese.

dinner.name: Mititei (Grilled Meat Rolls)
instructions: Mix meats with spices and broth
Shape into small cylinders
Grill over charcoal until browned
Serve with mustard and bread

dinner.name: Mujdei de Usturoi (Garlic Sauce)
instructions: Mujdei is Moldova's garlic sauce — pounded or blended until smooth
Crush or pound garlic with salt — the salt helps break down the garlic
Add oil gradually — like making a garlic aioli but without egg
Add a small amount of water or cold broth to adjust consistency
The result should be very pungent, white-ish, smooth
Mujdei is served alongside grilled meats, fish, mamaliga
The amount of garlic is not restrained — this is a sauce for garlic lovers
Moldova's garlic consumption is among Eastern Europe's highest
The mujdei is on every Moldovan table at every grill event
A piece of grilled meat without mujdei is incomplete in Moldova
dinner.description: Moldova's indispensable garlic sauce — crushed garlic pounded with salt and emulsified with oil, intensely pungent and white. Served alongside every grilled meat, fish, and mamaliga. Moldova's garlic consumption is among Eastern Europe's highest; no grill event is complete without mujdei. Similar to Ukrainian and Romanian garlic sauces — the Eastern European garlic condiment tradition.

dinner.name: Plăcinte cu Varza (Cabbage Pastry)
instructions: Make a soft, yeasted pastry dough — let rise 1 hour
Sauté shredded cabbage with onion until soft and slightly caramelized
Season with salt, pepper, dill
The filling should be slightly sweet from the caramelized cabbage
Roll dough thin, cut into circles or rectangles
Place cabbage filling inside, fold over and seal
Bake or fry — both are made in Moldova
Baked plăcinte are lighter; fried are richer and crispier
Plăcinte are Moldova's most universal food — every grandmother makes them
Fillings vary: cabbage, potato, cherry, pumpkin — cabbage is the classic savory version
Street vendors sell plăcinte everywhere in Chisinau
dinner.description: Moldova's grandmothers' pastry — soft yeasted dough filled with caramelized cabbage, either baked or fried. Plăcinte are the most universal Moldovan food: every family makes them, street vendors sell them in every city, and the fillings (cabbage, potato, cherry, cottage cheese) change with season. The cabbage version is the classic savory foundation.

dinner.name: Mămăligă Prăjită (Fried Polenta Slices)
instructions: Day-old mamaliga firms completely — it can be sliced like bread
Slice the cold mamaliga into 1.5 cm slices
Fry in butter or oil — medium heat
The polenta slices develop a golden, crispy crust on each side
The interior warms and softens
Top with crumbled brânza — it melts slightly from the heat
Smetana alongside
Fried mamaliga is the leftover transformation — nothing is wasted
The crispy polenta exterior against the soft interior and sharp cheese is entirely different from fresh mamaliga
Moldovan zero-waste cooking: the same maize porridge eaten twice, completely differently
The fried version is actually preferred by many — the crust adds a dimension
dinner.description: Moldova's leftover transformation — day-old mamaliga sliced thick and fried in butter until golden-crusted, topped with brânza and smetana. The crispy exterior and soft interior is a completely different experience from fresh mamaliga. Zero-waste Moldovan cooking: the same polenta eaten twice in different forms, both excellent.

snacks.name: Covrigi (Pretzels)
instructions: Make dough, rise 1 hour
Shape into pretzel form
Boil briefly, then bake at 200°C 15 min
Top with seeds

snacks.name: Covrigi (Pretzel-Style Bread)
instructions: Make a yeasted dough — similar to a pretzel dough
Let rise 1 hour
Shape into rings or pretzel shapes
The traditional ring (covrigi) is a Moldovan street food shape
Boil briefly in baking soda water — this gives the chewy exterior and deep brown color
Bake at 220°C until dark golden
Optionally coat with sesame or poppy seeds before baking
Covrigi are sold at street vendors and bakeries everywhere in Moldova
The chewy, slightly salty exterior and airy interior is the covrigi pleasure
Eaten as a snack, at tea time, or throughout the day
Similar to a soft pretzel — the Moldovan street bread
snacks.description: Moldova's street bread ring — yeasted dough shaped into rings, briefly boiled in baking soda water (giving the characteristic chewy, dark crust), then baked. Similar to a German pretzel or Polish obwarzanek. Sold at street vendors and bakeries throughout Moldova. The baking-soda boiling bath is the technique that distinguishes covrigi from ordinary bread.

snacks.name: Murături (Pickled Vegetables)
ingredients: Cabbage, cucumbers, tomatoes, watermelon, peppers (various combinations)
Dill, garlic, horseradish root, oak leaves (tannins for crispness)
instructions: Moldovan murături are lacto-fermented, not vinegar-pickled — the distinction matters enormously
Salt brine (2-3% salt solution) preserves through fermentation
The oak leaves and horseradish provide tannins — keeping vegetables crisp during fermentation
Pack vegetables tightly in a crock or jar with dill, garlic
Pour salt brine over to submerge completely
Weight down so nothing floats
Ferment at room temperature 1-2 weeks — taste regularly
When pleasantly sour: move to cold cellar
Moldovan murături includes things others don't pickle: watermelon, green tomatoes, whole peppers
The cellar full of pickled crocks is Moldova's food security through winter
The sour, garlicky crunch is the counterpoint to every rich, fatty winter dish
snacks.description: Moldova's fermented vegetable cellar — cucumbers, cabbage, green tomatoes, watermelon, and peppers lacto-fermented in salt brine with dill, garlic, and oak leaves (for crispness). Not vinegar-pickled — the lactic acid fermentation creates a completely different sourness. The cellar full of fermenting crocks is Moldova's winter food security. Murături alongside fatty winter dishes is the necessary acid contrast.

snacks.name: Sunflower Seed Snack
instructions: Dry toast sunflower seeds in a pan or oven
The seeds toast evenly without oil — the natural fat in the seeds prevents sticking
Shell and eat — the cracking and eating of sunflower seeds is a leisure activity
Moldova grows enormous quantities of sunflowers — it's a major agricultural crop
The sunflower seed is the universal Moldovan/Eastern European/Russian leisure snack
Cracking shells and eating seeds is done while watching football, talking, sitting in the sun
The pile of shells around you tells how long you've been sitting
Bags of sunflower seeds are sold at every kiosk
The ritual of cracking seeds is as much the point as eating them
snacks.description: Moldova's leisure snack — dry-toasted sunflower seeds, cracked and eaten while watching football, talking in the sun, or sitting in a park. Moldova grows sunflowers at industrial scale. The ritual of cracking seed shells is part of the activity: the growing pile of shells marks relaxed time passing. Universal throughout Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

desserts.name: Cozonac (Sweet Bread)
instructions: Make rich dough, rise twice
Roll, spread walnut-cocoa filling
Roll up, place in loaf pan
Bake at 175°C 45 min
desserts.description: Swirled sweet bread with walnut-cocoa filling.

desserts.name: Gogoși (Fried Dough Balls)
instructions: Mix dough — soft, slightly sweet
If using yeast: rise 1 hour
If using baking powder: fry immediately
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil — or roll into balls
They puff as they fry
The exterior should be golden; inside soft and airy
Dust with powdered sugar
Serve with jam for dipping
Gogoși are Moldova's fried doughnuts — closest to French beignets
Made at fairs, markets, and at home for special occasions
The powdered sugar cloud when you bite into one is the moment
Every Eastern European country has its fried dough version — gogoși is Moldova's
desserts.description: Moldova's fried doughnuts — yeasted or baking powder dough fried until puffed and golden, generously dusted with powdered sugar, served with jam. Every Eastern European country has its fried dough equivalent (Polish pączki, Hungarian fánk, Romanian gogoși); Moldova's version is soft, airy, and powdered-sugar-heavy.

desserts.name: Vișinată (Sour Cherry Preserves)
ingredients: Sour cherries (Morello type — the Moldovan variety)
instructions: Moldova has exceptional sour cherry (vișine) orchards
The sour cherry season (June-July) is brief and intense
Combine sour cherries with equal weight sugar
Macerate overnight — the cherries release juice
Cook gently until sugar is dissolved and cherries are glossy
The syrup should be deep red and slightly thickened
Jar and seal — it keeps for a year
Vișinată is both a preserve (eaten with bread, cheese, yogurt)
And a drink base: diluted in cold water it becomes a refreshing sour cherry drink
And a flavoring: added to smetana, poured over mamaliga, or over ice cream
Moldova's most beloved fruit preserve — the sour cherry is Moldova's signature fruit
desserts.description: Moldova's sour cherry preserve — the most beloved fruit preserve in a country with exceptional sour cherry orchards. Made in June-July when cherries peak, macerated with sugar overnight, and gently cooked. Used three ways: eaten as preserve with bread or cheese, diluted into a refreshing sour cherry drink (vișinată), or poured warm over ice cream or mamaliga.

drinks.name: Moldovan Wine
instructions: Serve at room temp for reds
Chill whites
Moldova has one of the highest vineyard densities in the world
drinks.description: Wine from one of Europe's oldest winemaking regions.

drinks.name: Compot (Fruit Compote)
instructions: Simmer fruit with sugar and cinnamon
Let cool
Serve cold as drink with fruit

drinks.name: Vin de Casă (Home Wine)
ingredients: Grapes (the indigenous Moldovan varieties: Feteasca Negra, Rara Neagra)
instructions: Moldova is one of the world's oldest wine-producing countries — wine culture goes back 5,000 years
Moldova has the world's largest wine cellars (Mileștii Mici — UNESCO recognized)
Every Moldovan family that has vines makes home wine (vin de casă)
Home wine is not inferior — it is the original, personal wine
Press grapes, ferment with natural wild yeast on the grape skins
Rack off skins after 1-2 weeks (for red) or immediately (for white)
Ferment in large glass vessels until dry
Bottle when clear
Home wine is offered to every guest before commercial wine
The personal nature of vin de casă — made by your family, from your vines — is its value
Moldova's Feteasca Neagra (Black Maiden) is one of Eastern Europe's finest indigenous red grapes
drinks.description: Moldova's personal wine — made in every household with a vineyard, fermented with wild grape yeast in glass vessels. Moldova has 5,000 years of wine history and the world's largest wine cellars (Mileștii Mici). The Feteasca Neagra grape is Moldova's finest indigenous variety. Home wine is offered to every guest before commercial wine — its personal origin is its value.
